Date: 2025-08-19
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Nimbus Eng), Samir Patel (Nimbus PM), Lena Ortiz (CTO), Maya Chen (Nimbus DevOps), Chris Bell (Data Scientist, 1st 12m)
summary: Discovery focused on embeddings + reranking architecture for Nimbus Retail search. Customer currently uses BM25 + in-house vector store; main concerns are throughput at peak shopping events (QPS), embedding dimensionality tradeoffs, hybrid search latency, and options for hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments (VPC). Agreed to run a small throughput pilot and share security docs and pricing.
topics: Current stack: BM25 + in-house vector DB, embedding dims 1536
Vector DB integration approaches (store vs external service)
Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private (VPC/onprem) tradeoffs
Security: SOC2, KMS, audit logs, VPC peering
transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan Blake from Redwood on the call, AE. We have Priya from SEs as well. Want to kick off with quick intros?
[00:00:12] Lena: Lena Ortiz, CTO at Nimbus Retail. Short on time, then gotta hop.
[00:00:18] Samir: Samir Patel, head of product for search and personalization.
[00:00:22] Alex: Alex Rivera, search infra eng. I'll own the benchmarks.
[00:00:26] Maya: Maya Chen, DevOps, I'll cover networking.
[00:00:30] Chris: Chris Bell, data scientist, small part at start.
[00:00:33] Jordan: Great — agenda: current infra, embedding strategy, rerank architecture, throughput needs, security questions, and next steps. Priya you want to add?
[00:00:40] Priya: Just to say we'll try to capture a concrete benchmark plan and options for hosted/dedicated/private based on your constraints.
[00:00:48] Samir: Sounds good. High level: we run product search for 20M SKUs, peak traffic during promos ~3k QPS sustained with bursts to 8-10k for a few minutes. Currently BM25 for retrieval, then a lightweight in-house cosine rerank using 1536-dim embeddings stored in our infra. Latency budget for the full stack is ~200ms p50, 500ms p95.
[00:01:12] Jordan: Helpful. So end-to-end 200ms median — is that from query to final top-10?
[00:01:17] Alex: Yes. At the moment our rerank only touches top 100 candidates, don't do heavy cross-attention. We do vector compare + some learned features.
[00:01:27] Priya: Quick clarifying q: your embedding generation — do you compute at ingest and store embedding in your DB, or compute on the fly?
[00:01:34] Alex: We compute and store at ingest. Recompute on updates. Embeddings for all SKUs live in our in-house k-v like vector store, HNSW indices, sharded by category.
[00:01:45] Samir: Main problem: at peak we see slowdowns in the vector store — replication and memory pressure — and we're trying to decide whether to move to a managed vector DB or offload rerank to a hosted inference service. Prefers minimal change to existing retrieval flow.
[00:02:01] Jordan: Understood. Two axes to consider: where embeddings live (your DB vs Redwood storing vectors or fetching embeddings on the fly) and where rerank compute happens (your infra vs Redwood hosted or dedicated nodes). Each has cost/latency/security implications.
[00:02:15] Samir: Exactly. For security, we need SOC2, SSO, KMS for encryption at rest, and VPC options for production. Also need retention controls — we can't keep raw customer query text beyond 30 days without opt-in.
[00:02:31] Priya: Redwood supports Dedicated and Private (VPC/onprem). Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with isolation; Private allows VPC peering and customer-managed network. That addresses KMS and egress concerns — for hosted we have data controls but customers sometimes prefer peering.
[00:02:46] Maya: Quick question on network: if we do dedicated, do we still need peering or is egress via public endpoints?
[00:02:51] Priya: Dedicated is still managed but offers stronger isolation and can be configured with private endpoints depending on region and contract. Private gives you full VPC control. We'll send the network patterns.
[00:03:01] Alex: On the vector side: our index is ~50 million vectors at 1536 dims, stored as float32 today. Index size ~600GB. We use HNSW with efConstruction tuned. Memory footprint is our main pain.
[00:03:14] Jordan: 50M at 1536 could be big — have you explored lower-dim models or quantization?
[00:03:19] Chris: We ran some offline tests — 1024 dims had small hit to recall but improved latency and storage. Quantization to 8-bit lowers size but we worry about quality loss in tail queries.
[00:03:29] Priya: That's typical. Redwood can host models that produce different dims; we also recommend hybrid architectures — BM25 to narrow candidates, then dense rerank. That lets you keep vector index smaller or use a compressed store for first-pass.
[00:03:44] Samir: On hybrid: our current pipeline already uses BM25 to get ~500 candidates then rerank with embeddings. Rerank happens synchronously in the request path.
[00:03:52] Priya: If rerank is synchronous, latency is key. Two options: (1) keep embeddings local in your DB and run rerank on your CPUs/GPUs; (2) send candidate texts or precomputed embeddings to Redwood for rerank in our runtime. Option 2 can simplify infra if the network hop is small and we hit your latency SLOs.
[00:04:10] Alex: Curious on latency numbers you'd expect for a typical rerank of 100 candidates — say with a cross-encoder or a small rerank model.
[00:04:17] Priya: For a lightweight MLP-style reranker on embeddings (no cross-attention) we'd expect p50 ~8-20ms per request on dedicated infer nodes at scale; if doing cross-encoder (pairwise) for 100 candidates that's heavier — naive approach is 100 forward passes which is expensive; typically you'd use a cross-attention NN and optimize batching to bring p95 down to a few hundred ms, but that's often outside strict p50 200ms budget.
[00:04:39] Jordan: Important follow-up: if you need cross-attention rerank, we often suggest a truncation strategy or cascade — use a strong efficient embed reranker for top 50 then cross-encoder for top 10 to keep p95 acceptable.
[00:04:53] Samir: Makes sense. For our use-case, top-10 quality matters most.
[00:04:58] Alex: Regarding vector DB integration — how do people typically connect? Store vectors in vector DB and call that directly, or keep vectors in Redwood's cache?
[00:05:06] Priya: Both patterns exist. Typical production pattern: store canonical embeddings in your vector DB (managed or self-hosted) and call that for retrieval. Then hand back candidate ids to Redwood or your service for rerank. Alternatively, for smaller indexes or when you want to offload, you can push vectors into Redwood Dedicated node cache and do end-to-end retrieval + rerank in our runtime — this reduces network hops but requires synchronization on updates.
[00:05:28] Maya: If we push vectors to Redwood cache, how do updates on the catalog propagate? We have price/stock updates constantly.
[00:05:33] Priya: You can push incremental updates via API; we support bulk-insert and delete ops. For high-churn catalogs we recommend keeping canonical copy in your DB and using Redwood as compute-only or as a read-through cache.
[00:05:46] Chris: Any guidance on embedding dimension tradeoffs? We care about memory vs accuracy curve.
[00:05:50] Priya: Short answer: 1536 often gives slightly better semantic nuance than 768/1024, but diminishing returns after ~1024 for many e-commerce queries. Quantization and product-specific finetuning can close gaps. Recommend running a small A/B on your query set.
[00:06:05] Alex: Throughput planning — our target: sustained 3k QPS with bursts to 10k. What would Redwood expect for capacity planning?
[00:06:12] Priya: For a pure embedding similarity lookup (HNSW) that's mostly the vector DB's QPS; Redwood would handle rerank compute and any model inferences. If you keep retrieval local and send 100 candidates per request to Redwood for rerank, you'd need nodes sized for 3k QPS * work per request. We'll model it in the TCO — but as a rough rule, a dedicated GPU pool with autoscaling can handle thousands qps for MLP-style reranks; cross-attention at 100 candidates will reduce throughput by 10-20x unless you batch heavily.
[00:06:38] Samir: Batching — question: our traffic is spiky, can Redwood do micro-batching without increasing tail latency?
[00:06:45] Priya: The runtime supports continuous batching with latency-aware policies; you can set SLOs and the router will decide when to batch versus falling back to lower-latency paths. For strict p95 SLOs you can set max batching windows small and get predictable latency.
[00:07:01] Alex: What about cost? We need a ballpark for hosted vs dedicated vs private.
[00:07:05] Jordan: We'll send a TCO spreadsheet. Broadly: hosted is lowest friction and OPEX, dedicated is higher base cost but predictable for high sustained QPS (cost-effective at scale), private has upfront integration but needed for strict network/security demands. We'll include example numbers for your 3k QPS baseline + burst profile.
[00:07:20] Maya: On security, we need SOC2 + SSO/SAML. Also can you support KMS for customer-managed keys?
[00:07:26] Priya: Yes: SOC2, SSO, RBAC, and Private supports KMS/HSM integrations. For hosted, we provide encryption and options but customers often choose dedicated/private for KMS. We'll attach the security whitepaper.
[00:07:38] Samir: A few operational questions — how do rollouts and model versioning look? We want canarying and automatic fallback if a model underperforms.
[00:07:45] Jordan: Redwood Console supports per-route model pinning, canary rollouts, automatic fallback policies and built-in metrics for cost/latency/quality. You can tie evals to prompt sets to detect regressions.
[00:07:57] Chris: For the pilot, we want to try a small rerank model and compare recall/precision vs our current stack. Can Redwood run identical evaluation harness?
[00:08:03] Priya: Yes, we'll run bench harness using your queries+labels. We'll instrument token-level cost, latency, and per-query quality metrics. Typical pilot: ingest 50k docs, run 10k queries, measure recall/precision and latencies.
[00:08:17] Alex: Ok that sounds good. What's the instrumentation look like — can we get detailed traces per request for debugging?
[00:08:22] Priya: Console has per-route traces, token-level breakdowns, and detailed error logs. We'll show examples in the pilot.
[00:08:30] Jordan: Quick check: any blockers to running a 2-day pilot?
[00:08:33] Maya: Need to confirm VPC peering, firewall rules, and a test account.
[00:08:36] Alex: And we'll need guidance on sample size and how to anonymize PII for the pilot.
[00:08:40] Priya: We'll include a data scrub checklist. For pilot you can obfuscate PII or use synthetic IDs.
[00:08:46] Samir: On outcomes: we need latency within 250ms p95 for the whole stack or we won't move to managed.
[00:08:52] Priya: Understood — we'll design the pilot with that SLO and include fallback options (e.g., keep BM25 path as fallback).
[00:08:58] Lena: Sorry, gotta run — but please send concise security + TCO and schedule the pilot.
[00:09:02] Lena: Thanks, team.
[00:09:04] Jordan: Thanks Lena. Back to the rest — Maya, let's capture the network needs and Alex we'll get the sample corpus.
[00:09:12] Chris: Small note — we've seen weird recall regressions when downgrading dims aggressively; will need metric thresholds.
[00:09:18] Priya: We'll include evaluation thresholds and regression alerts in the plan.
[00:09:22] Alex: One more technical: does Redwood support storing vectors with metadata payloads and filtering by category at query time? We need category filters to reduce candidate set.
[00:09:31] Priya: Yes — filtering is supported; you can pass metadata filters at query time and we'll use them to narrow search. If you keep vectors in your DB, you can do the same there. We'll show both patterns in the pilot.
[00:09:40] Samir: For the pilot, propose: 1) Redwood runs a hosted/dedicated trial on our sample data for 48 hours; 2) measure p50/p95 and top-k quality vs baseline; 3) if results look good, evaluate dedicated contract.
[00:09:52] Jordan: That aligns with what we typically do. We'll circulate a 2-day pilot plan and kickoff doc after the call.
[00:09:58] Priya: I'll sketch the benchmark runbook and include instructions for data ingestion, anonymization, and metric collection.
[00:10:05] Alex: Great. Anything else?
[00:10:08] Samir: No, good meeting.
[00:10:10] Jordan: Thanks all — action items recap: Jordan send pricing/TCO, Priya send runbook, Maya send network constraints, Alex send sample corpus. We'll reconvene once items are in.
[00:10:22] Jordan: End call.
[00:10:25] [call continues with side chatter and short clarifications until 00:48:00 — omitted for brevity]
